# Git Merge vs Git Rebase

## What They Do

**`git merge`** combines two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that has two parents, preserving the exact history of how development happened.

**`git rebase`** moves your commits to a new base, replaying them one by one on top of another branch, rewriting history to appear linear.

---

## Visual Comparison

**Starting point:**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                      \
feature:               D --- E
```

**After `git merge main` (from feature):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C --------\
                      \         \
feature:               D --- E --- M   ← merge commit with 2 parents
```

**After `git rebase main` (from feature):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                      \
feature:               D' --- E'   ← commits replayed, new hashes
```

---

## When to Use Each

### Use `git merge` when:
- Merging a **completed feature into main/develop**
- Working on a **shared/public branch** others are using
- You want to **preserve exact history** (auditing, compliance)
- The branch has **many contributors**
- You want to clearly mark **when a feature was integrated**

### Use `git rebase` when:
- **Updating a local feature branch** with upstream changes
- You want a **clean, linear history** before merging
- Working on a **private branch** no one else has
- Doing **interactive rebase** to clean up messy commits before review
- Squashing "WIP" commits into logical units

---

## The Tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves exact truth | Rewrites for clarity |
| Commits | Adds a merge commit | Replays commits (new hashes) |
| Conflicts | Resolved once | May resolve per-commit |
| Safety | Safe on shared branches | **Dangerous on shared branches** |
| Readability | Can get noisy | Clean linear history |
| Blame/bisect | Accurate timestamps | Easier to follow |

---

## The Golden Rule of Rebase

> **Never rebase a branch that others are working on.**

When you rebase, commits get new SHA hashes. If someone else has the old commits, their history diverges from yours and you'll create a mess.

```bash
# SAFE - your local feature branch
git checkout feature/my-work
git rebase main

# DANGEROUS - shared branch others have pulled
git rebase main shared-team-branch  # ← don't do this
```

---

## Common Workflows

**Keeping a feature branch up to date:**
```bash
git checkout feature/my-work
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main    # cleaner than merging main into feature
```

**Interactive rebase to clean up before PR:**
```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~4      # squash/reword last 4 commits
```

**Merging a finished feature:**
```bash
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature/my-work   # --no-ff preserves the merge commit
```

---

## My Recommendation

A practical middle ground used by many teams:

1. **Rebase locally** to keep your feature branch current and history clean
2. **Merge** (or squash merge) into main when the feature is done
3. **Never rebase** after pushing to a shared remote branch

This gives you clean history without the collaboration risks of rewriting shared history.
